strengths: Novel perspective on viewing Rashomon sets as policy objects rather than theoretical constructs, grounded in realistic ML governance scenarios
Comprehensive multi-dimensional analysis simultaneously addressing robustness, privacy, stability, and interpretability
Solid theoretical contributions with correct proofs (Theorems 1-6) characterizing single-model vulnerabilities and set-level properties
Clear presentation of core robustness-privacy trade-off with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 5)
Consistent empirical validation across 6 datasets demonstrating predicted phenomena using appropriate statistical methods
Practical governance angle connecting theoretical results to institutions' policy decisions
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: essentially all experiments use TreeFARMS on sparse decision trees; claims about hypothesis-space-agnostic results unsubstantiated; unclear if findings extend to neural networks or modern ML models that dominate practice

Reactive robustness concept underdeveloped: lacks practical feasibility (how to identify which model to switch to?), assumes adversaries attack single models only, requires specific diversity structures (angular distance) that may not naturally emerge in Rashomon sets

Privacy analysis has fundamental issues: conflates distributional leakage (KL divergence) with membership privacy; uses non-standard reconstruction-error metric rather than membership inference; Theorem 5's argument that similar Rashomon sets protect membership privacy lacks rigor and formal privacy guarantees

Stability Theorem 4 has very restrictive conditions (KL(D||D') ≤ ε²/8 becomes ~10⁻⁶ for typical ε=0.01); Theorem 5 is empirical-only with no theoretical characterization of when stability holds; limited practical guidance
Theorem 2 oversimplified with strong assumptions (binary features, L₀ perturbations, majority-label prediction); lower bound is loose; limited connection to modern adversarial robustness literature

Trade-off analysis lacks actionable guidance: Figure 5 shows trade-off but provides no decision rule; casually mentioned 'intermediate regime' deserves rigorous characterization; no Pareto frontier analysis or cost-benefit framework
Information-theoretic bounds are loose (e.g., Theorem 1 uses standard counting argument); constants hidden in O(·) notation

Experimental limitations: small reconstruction-attack datasets (100 points), only 6 UCI datasets, binarization of continuous features, only one Rashomon-set construction algorithm (TreeFARMS), no comparison with other multi-model approaches
Missing practical guidance: how to construct diverse Rashomon sets with desired properties?, which diversity metrics matter for which threat models?, computational costs of maintaining large sets?

Missing key analyses: sensitivity to Rashomon parameter ε, three-way accuracy-robustness-privacy trade-offs, impact of model-selection bias on privacy, comparison with single robust models or differential-privacy baselines

strengths: Addresses practically important problem of governance-level thinking about Rashomon sets rather than single models
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six datasets with careful ablations of sampling strategies and honest verification of theoretical predictions
Clear articulation and visualization of the robustness-privacy trade-off through Table 1 and Figure 1
Honest treatment of limitations, including distinction between distributional leakage and membership privacy
Systematic examination of multiple trustworthiness dimensions (robustness, stability, privacy) in unified framework
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual theoretical results (Theorems 1-6) are straightforward combinations of existing techniques (entropy bounds, margin-based analysis, Pinsker's inequality) without deep new insights

Severely narrow scope: empirical analysis restricted to sparse decision trees via TreeFARMS on small tabular datasets (<10k samples); unclear generalization to modern ML (neural networks, gradient-boosting, large-scale domains)

Incomplete characterization of core claim: the robustness-privacy trade-off is demonstrated empirically but no formal conditions established for when/why it occurs or whether it is fundamental or avoidable
Weak adversarial attacks: L₀ perturbations with budget 1 on binarized 4-dimensional data are toy scenarios; no adaptive attacks or gradient-based methods
Problematic privacy analysis: relies on distributional leakage (KL divergence) and reconstruction attacks rather than standard membership inference; bounds in Theorem 6 are loose for small δ
Reactive robustness assumes non-adaptive attackers; unclear how model rotation works in practice or how adaptive adversaries affect defense strategy
Theorem 4-6 stated as hypothesis-space agnostic but proved only for specific model classes, undermining generality claims
Incomplete experimental design: no comparison with differential privacy or robust training methods; limited ablation on sensitivity to Rashomon parameter ε and other hyperparameters
Policy recommendations are vague ('balance transparency with privacy') rather than actionable, lacking concrete mechanisms for diversity-aware disclosure
Loose theoretical bounds: Theorem 2 lower bound depends heavily on class imbalance; Theorem 6 denominator term can become very loose for boundary distributions

strengths: Novel framing of Rashomon sets as policy objects for governance with clear practical relevance to real ML deployments
Comprehensive theoretical analysis spanning robustness, stability, and privacy with formal theorems (Theorems 1-6) supporting key claims
Clear identification and empirical validation of fundamental robustness-privacy trade-off across multiple datasets with consistent findings
Well-motivated introduction and generally clear presentation with good intuition for technical results
Novel conceptual contributions including 'reactive robustness' and analysis of how model diversity affects trustworthiness properties
weaknesses: Limited theoretical scope: results apply primarily to sparse trees with binary features/labels; generalization to modern architectures (neural networks) and continuous spaces unclear
All experiments focus on sparse decision trees via TreeFARMS; lack of validation on linear models (despite theory) and other architectures severely limits impact
Privacy analysis focuses on distributional leakage (KL divergence) rather than membership privacy; relationship between Theorems 5 and 6 (which point in opposite directions) underdeveloped
Limited practical guidance on resolving the robustness-privacy trade-off; 'sweet spot' identified empirically but not theoretically characterized, with location varying across datasets
Theorem 4 (distribution shift stability) has restrictive KL condition (ε²/8) with limited practical guidance; Theorem 2 assumes specific rule list structure making it illustrative rather than general
Privacy evaluation uses reconstruction error as proxy rather than membership inference attacks, limiting threat model; DRAFT is one specific attack with unclear generalization
Theorems support individual claims but don't yield unified characterization of core robustness-privacy trade-off; connection between different results could be clearer

strengths: Novel formalization of the robustness-privacy trade-off at the Rashomon set level with important practical implications for ML deployment
Rigorous theoretical framework with multiple formally proven theorems (4.1, 4.2, 5.1-5.6) backed by complete proofs in appendices

Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 datasets, multiple model types (decision trees, linear models, neural networks), and diverse attack scenarios (reconstruction, membership inference, adversarial)
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (particularly Figure 1), and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Practical contribution of frameworks for operationalizing robustness-privacy trade-offs (Section 6.4, Appendix E.8) with hybrid selection algorithms
Attention to both theoretical and empirical aspects with experiments validating theoretical predictions across different settings
weaknesses: Theoretical scope limited to 0-1 loss for binary classification with decision trees; extension to multi-class, continuous losses, and modern architectures (high-dimensional neural networks) remains unclear

Limited practical actionability: proposed solutions rely on heuristic thresholds without clear guidance for practitioners; no systematic methodology for selecting appropriate robustness-privacy trade-off points
Gap between theory (discrete models) and practice (continuous, high-dimensional models): neural network experiments limited to 2-layer networks with 8-20 hidden units
Privacy analysis uses heuristic measures (reconstruction error, membership inference) rather than formal privacy definitions like differential privacy; no connection to certified privacy guarantees

Restricted assumptions: Theorem 5.5 requires Rashomon sets from different datasets to be nearly identical; assumption about bounded loss functions and specific singular value properties limits generalizability

Experimental limitations: datasets modest in size (max ~50k samples), DRAFT reconstruction attack not state-of-the-art, membership inference uses basic KL-divergence without sophisticated attacks, missing comparisons with differential privacy and other privacy-preserving ensemble methods
Core insight that diversity improves robustness while increasing information leakage is somewhat intuitive; limited novelty in the fundamental observation

Underdeveloped governance aspects: 'Rashomon set as policy object' framing introduced but not systematically developed; missing clear recommendations for practitioners or regulators on handling robustness-privacy tension

strengths: Addresses an important and timely topic at the intersection of interpretability, robustness, and privacy in machine learning
Provides rigorous theoretical analysis with formal theorems and complete proofs characterizing the dual nature of Rashomon sets
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 datasets, multiple model types, and various attack scenarios
Clear visualizations and figures effectively communicate the robustness-privacy trade-offs
Goes beyond pure theory to discuss practical operationalization challenges and proposes concrete algorithms
weaknesses: Core insight that diversity improves robustness but increases privacy leakage is intuitive and unsurprising, limiting novelty
Significant gap between theory and practice: theoretical results restricted to binary decision trees and linear models; extension to neural networks underdeveloped
Experimental scope limited to dated, small-scale datasets (UCI 2017, COMPAS 2016, FICO 2018) with primary focus on decision trees; neural network experiments relegated to appendices
Central claims oversimplified: privacy-robustness trade-off presented as universal but shown to be highly dataset and model-dependent; stability results apply only under restrictive conditions
Theorem 4.2 assumes very specific attack constraints (binary features, bounded ℓ∞ perturbations) that don't generalize; Theorem 5.6's information leakage bounds are loose and dataset-dependent
Limited concrete mitigation strategies offered; proposed privacy-first framework barely evaluated; hybrid selection algorithm uses unjustified heuristic thresholds (35% tolerance)
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided, scattered implementation details, insufficient hyperparameter justification, non-standard DRAFT attack setup
Incomplete related work: limited engagement with ensemble diversity and certified robustness literature; no comparison with standard privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy
Dense presentation makes the paper challenging to follow; key messages not clearly stated upfront; scope limited to tabular classification data with unclear generalization to other domains

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: the dual nature of Rashomon sets for trustworthiness, demonstrating that diversity improves robustness while increasing privacy risks
Comprehensive theoretical framework with multiple rigorous theorems (4.1-5.6) characterizing robustness-privacy-stability tradeoffs, supported by complete proofs
Extensive empirical validation across 6 real datasets with multiple experimental scenarios (adversarial robustness, information leakage, stability) thoroughly supporting theoretical claims
Practical framework for operationalizing the robustness-privacy tradeoff with actionable guidance for practitioners selecting ensemble sizes
Well-executed research combining solid methodology, clear presentation with effective visualizations, comprehensive appendices, and honest limitations discussion
Novel insights about how individual model sparsity affects privacy while simultaneously enabling vulnerability to targeted attacks
weaknesses: Limited scope of model classes: experiments primarily on decision trees using TreeFARMS; generalizability to other architectures (neural networks, boosting methods, ensembles) unclear, with only preliminary neural network experiments

Somewhat incremental contribution: the dual-edged nature of diversity is partially intuitive; the paper primarily formalizes and empirically validates this intuition rather than discovering fundamentally unexpected phenomena

Privacy measurement limitations: reconstruction error (DRAFT) is the primary privacy metric; other privacy notions (differential privacy, formal privacy guarantees) and stronger membership inference attacks could be examined
Strong theoretical assumptions: Theorem 5.1 assumes model independence, Theorem 5.5 assumes substantial overlap between neighboring Rashomon sets, and Theorem 5.6 lacks full rigor for neural networks
Limited adversarial evaluation: attacks use relatively simple threat models (fixed budget η=0.1); simultaneous attack evaluation limited to 10 trees due to computational constraints

Practical operationalization underexplored: guidance for practitioners on selecting ensemble sizes and operating points on Pareto frontier could be more rigorous; privacy-first selection rule (E.6) and hybrid algorithm (E.8) feel somewhat ad-hoc
Missing reproducibility aid: no mention of code release; while methodology is clear, availability of implementation would strengthen reproducibility
